body.text: As the European summer comes to an end, an intriguing question emerges. Will the record-breaking heat and wildfires that have devastated the continent over the past four months make any difference to governments’ commitments to tackling climate change?

A succession of heatwaves from May to August saw the highest-ever temperatures recorded in most of Europe: 45C in Spain and Italy, 44C in France, 42C in Germany, 38C in Britain. Nearly 2000 wildfires have consumed more than 650,000 hectares, forcing hundreds of thousands of people from their homes in southern Europe, Belgium and Britain. Heat is estimated to have caused more than 35,000 deaths. Dried-out rivers have closed nuclear power stations and halted waterborne transport. Agricultural production is sharply down and food prices are up.

Each day more climate-related devastation plays out somewhere in the world. The mudslides in Nepal and Tibet last month, which have killed more than 1200 people and left 5000 missing, were caused by melting glaciers almost certainly exacerbated by warmer temperatures. Canada’s nearly 5000 wildfires have covered more than four million hectares in the past few months, with at least 500 still burning; the resulting air pollution has reached as far south as Philadelphia. More than 700,000 people were recently evacuated in southern China after the third typhoon in a month brought torrential rain. India has hit new heat records for four of the past five years, with temperatures of up to 48C becoming routine in the north of the country. In May, ninety-seven of the one hundred hottest cities in the world were recorded in the country.

Scientists are no longer reluctant to attribute individual extreme weather events to climate change. World Weather Attribution said Europe’s record-breaking temperatures would have been “virtually impossible” fifty years ago, and “climate change is unequivocally to blame.”

And more is to come. Climate change is a trend, not an event. The UN Environment Programme said last week that the Paris agreement target of limiting warming to 1.5C is now out of reach, with 1.8C the minimum achievable. While 1.5C shouldn’t be abandoned, it is now only possible through “overshoot and return,” requiring an unlikely but not impossible net negative emissions in the second half of the century. This year is shaping up globally to be the hottest year ever — not least due to the “supersized” El Niño phenomenon now building — but in a decade’s time it will look merely normal.

The European public has taken the point. In its annual survey of global public opinion to be published next month, the Climate Opinion Research Exchange has found a significant rise over the past year in the number of people who believe climate change “is making other crises in my country worse”; and the number who include it in their list of top three most important political issues has risen sharply this summer in France, Spain, Italy and Britain.

These figures certainly raise climate change’s political salience (as the psephologists put it), but they still represent less than 25 per cent of voters in most countries (less than 35 per cent in France). Voters who don’t think climate is one of the issues most in need of political attention still greatly outnumber those who do.
It’s worth probing these figures a little more deeply, for they help to explain the new politics of global warming in Europe.

Britain is an instructive case. New polling by YouGov, again not yet published, has just under a quarter of all British voters putting the environment or climate change in their top three political issues. But among Labour voters this rises to 37 per cent, putting it above traditionally important issues such as crime and housing. And with Labour voters ranging from young metropolitan graduates and professionals to the working-class residents of former industrial and mining towns, it matters how these voters split.

Of Labour voters who say they might otherwise vote Green, 49 per cent put the environment in their top three issues. For those who might otherwise vote for Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform UK that number drops to only 6 per cent. Environment and climate are most important to eighteen- to twenty-four-year-olds, to professionals and those who voted to remain in the European Union in the 2016 Brexit referendum. They are least important to over sixty-fives, to manual workers and those who voted to leave the EU.

As might be expected, the higher salience of climate change as an issue has made more people favourable to climate policies. But only by two to three percentage points. And most of those who are more supportive of climate action are people who were already supportive. The number of former opponents of climate action who have been persuaded by the evidence of climate change to change their mind on policy seems to be very small.

These voter positions are starkly reflected in the political parties’ positioning. Taking its cue from Trump’s MAGA movement, Reform UK has made climate scepticism and anti-climate policy a central plank of its platform. It regards concerns about global warming and support for renewable energy as another way in which the “woke” liberal elite has imposed crippling costs on ordinary people and businesses. Reform calls Britain’s 2050 emissions goal “net stupid zero.”

This might have been expected; perhaps more surprising is the change in the mainstream Conservative Party. It was the Tories who, in government in 2019, put net zero by 2050 into law. Under the party’s relatively new leader Kemi Badenoch, not only has the net zero goal been jettisoned, so has the foundational 2008 Climate Change Act, which Badenoch has pledged to repeal. Any members who don’t support these new positions, she says, are no longer welcome in the party.

Two dynamics are going on here. On the one hand the Conservatives have decided to chase the same right-wing voters as Reform, and these voters are now much more climate-sceptic than the population at large. On the other, the opposition of these two parties to climate policy — and the increasingly vociferous campaigns being waged against it by the right-wing Daily Telegraph, Daily Mail and Sun, and TV channel GB News — have almost certainly made many of those voters more climate sceptical. Where once Britain had a cross-party consensus on climate action — and therefore, in many ways, not much political debate — now it is a fiercely contested field. In the social media feeds seen by those on the political right, anti-climate positions are dominant.

This phenomenon is mirrored across most of Europe. In Germany’s most recent regional election, in Saxony-Anhalt, the extreme right-wing Alternative für Deutschland, or AfD, got 44 per cent of the vote, and may form the next state government. Though its main political identity is anti-immigration, it is opposed to any policies to mitigate climate change, which it believes is a natural phenomenon; and if it took power at a national level (it is leading in the polls) it would pull Germany out of the Paris agreement. In France, the far-right National Rally has been less extreme but rejects what it describes as “punitive” ecological policies, including such things as support for renewable energy.

This ideological and cultural backlash on the right has coincided with a concerted campaign by business to weaken European climate policy on economic grounds. Hit hard by the rise in energy costs caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and facing aggressive competition from China and the US, European manufacturers have attacked green policies as anti-jobs. Having successfully got the EU’s electric vehicle mandate watered down at the end of last year, Germany is now seeking, this time with France’s help, to reduce the stringency of the EU’s flagship Emissions Trading Scheme, under which industrial companies must buy carbon permits to cover their emissions. The EU’s 2030 and 2040 emissions targets remain intact, and its president Ursula von der Leyen is still seeking to accelerate the electrification of its economy in response to fossil fuel volatility. But the pressures on climate policy are mounting.

In Britain two big decisions are coming up which will reveal where the balance of power lies between pro-green and anti-green political forces. The first is on the approval of licences for oil and gas production. In its 2024 election manifesto Labour pledged that, as part of its global commitment to 1.5C, it would not grant any new drilling licences. But two existing ones have now come up for re-approval after the courts ruled their environmental impact assessments flawed.

The issue has become a touchstone for both climate campaigners and trade unionists. Environmentalists argue it should be unthinkable to go ahead with new fossil fuel production after a summer which has demonstrated the deadly impacts of climate change. The unions, along with most of the media, say it would be madness not to produce more oil and gas domestically, rather than importing it, at a time of global energy insecurity.

A similar argument is brewing over a government proposal to weaken Britain’s zero-emissions vehicle, or ZEV, mandate, which requires auto manufacturers to sell a rising proportion of EVs. UK-based manufacturers have complained the public are not buying enough EVs and want the phasing out of petrol and diesel cars — due by 2030, with hybrids phased out by 2035 — to be slowed down. Climate campaigners point out Britain is more or less completely dependent on EVs to meet its statutory emissions targets over the next decade; if the policy is watered down, it will either not meet its targets, or only at much higher cost to the economy and consumers.

Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, will need to make decisions on both these issues soon. Climate activists fear the worst. Despite the unprecedented temperatures, Burnham has so far barely mentioned climate change and insists he wants to be “pragmatic” on oil and gas, which is widely read as code for “we should grant those licences.” On the ZEV, the green side of the argument won’t be helped by this week’s announcement of 4000 job losses at one of Britain’s biggest manufacturers, Jaguar Land Rover, due to falling sales.

Yet Burnham will be aware of those polling numbers. He became prime minister in July after winning a by-election in a former mining town in Greater Manchester in which, in local elections just a few weeks before, Reform had won almost half the vote. But next month he faces a by-election in inner London — precipitated by the resignation from parliament of former prime minister Keir Starmer — in which Labour is under serious threat from the Green Party. If on these two issues he comes out on the side of jobs and against climate action he may win support among Reform-leaning voters. But he will be giving seats in London and other urban areas to the Greens.

And there are more prospective Green voters among Labour supporters than Reform ones. In the English local elections in May, Labour shed more than half of those who had voted for it in the 2024 general election. But many more switched to the Greens (22 per cent) and the green-tinged Liberal Democrats (16 per cent) than to Reform (6 per cent) or the Conservatives (5 per cent).

And the key point is this: for those Labour supporters who might vote Green or Lib Dem, climate change is a major motivation, but this is not the case for those who might vote Reform. It is Labour’s positioning on immigration that will largely determine which way Labour–Reform switchers will go. But these voters simply don’t care enough about climate change for the same to be true of its positioning on net zero. Labour–Green switchers, on the other hand, really do care. So leaning away from climate policy is likely to cost Labour many more votes than leaning into it.

In a few metropolitan areas, and especially in London, losing votes to the Greens means losing parliamentary seats to them in a general election. But in the rest of the country, under Britain’s first-past-the-post-electoral system, it means splitting the Labour vote and thereby allowing Reform or the Conservatives to win. Paradoxically, if Labour opposes climate action it is more likely to lose a general election to Reform.
The extreme heat of the last few months in Europe seems finally to have subsided. But for governments the politics of climate change may just be hotting up. •
